opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so the original AlphaGo actually had separate networks — a policy network and a value network, trained somewhat independently. With AlphaGo Zero they merged them into a single residual tower with two heads: one outputting a distribution over moves, the other outputting a scalar estimate of who's going to win. And the compute savings there are pretty significant, but I think the more interesting part is why it works at all.

On the pure compute side, the bulk of the cost is in the trunk — all those convolutional or residual layers that build up a representation of the board. The heads are tiny by comparison. So if you share the trunk, you're roughly halving the forward-pass cost at every node in the search. And that matters enormously in MCTS, because you're evaluating the network thousands of times per move. Any constant-factor saving per evaluation compounds directly into either faster play or deeper search for the same budget.

But the deeper point is that the two tasks want the same features. To know what a good move is, you need to understand which groups are alive, where the territory is, what's under threat. And to know who's winning, you need to understand… exactly the same things. So the representations are highly complementary, and training them jointly acts as a kind of regularizer. The value head in particular is prone to overfitting — you only get one bit of signal per game, the outcome — and the policy targets give much denser supervision that keeps the shared representation grounded. DeepMind reported that the combined "dual" network actually played better than the separate ones, not just cheaper.

I think that's a recurring lesson that shows up again in robotics and in language models: if two predictions depend on the same underlying understanding of the world, you usually want one model learning that understanding and multiple cheap readouts on top, rather than paying for the world model twice. The trick is knowing when tasks genuinely share structure versus when they'll fight each other for capacity — and in Go, policy and value are about as aligned as two objectives can get.

r001.rationale: The response says sharing the network trunk reduces the forward-pass cost and saves computation during repeated search evaluations.

r002.rationale: It says policy and value predictions rely on the same features and have aligned objectives, but does not clearly state that their evaluations of a position should be consistent.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so this is one of those things that sounds like an engineering footnote but actually tells you something about how the whole system works. In the original AlphaGo, you had separate networks for the policy and the value function, and then AlphaGo Zero merged them into a single trunk with two heads. The obvious win is you run the convolutional stack once per board position instead of twice, so you roughly halve the forward-pass cost during MCTS, and MCTS is where all the compute goes. Every leaf expansion needs both a prior over moves and an evaluation of the position, so if you're paying for two networks, you're paying twice at the exact bottleneck.

But I think the deeper point is that the compute savings aren't really the interesting part. The interesting part is that the shared representation made the model better, not just cheaper. When you force one set of features to serve both "what should I play here" and "who's winning," you get a regularization effect. The value head stops overfitting to the game outcomes, which are incredibly noisy, because the policy loss is anchoring the features to something more structured. DeepMind reported the combined network outperformed the separate ones, and I don't think that was a coincidence.

Where I'd push back a little on treating it as pure savings is that the two tasks don't always want the same thing. Policy is a local, "where's the next good move" question, and value is a global, "how does this whole board resolve" question. For Go they happen to be deeply correlated, so sharing works. In robotics, which is where I spend my time, you don't always get that luxury. You can have a policy head that wants fine-grained perceptual detail about a gripper contact and a value head that wants coarse task progress, and if you naively share a trunk, you can get negative transfer. So I think of the AlphaGo result as a lesson about the right inductive bias for that domain, rather than a universal rule that multi-task sharing is free compute.

The other thing I'd flag is that the savings compound with the search. A cheaper network means more simulations per second at a fixed budget, which means better move selection, which means better self-play data, which means a better network. So a factor of two in inference cost isn't just a factor of two in efficiency, it feeds back into the quality of the whole training loop.

r001.rationale: It says AlphaGo Zero’s shared trunk runs once instead of twice per position, roughly halving forward-pass cost during search.

r002.rationale: It says the policy and value tasks are correlated in Go and can benefit from shared features, but does not state that their predictions should provide consistent evaluations of a position.

astra-6.text:
The intuition is that choosing a move and evaluating a position require a lot of the same understanding of the board. You need to recognize things like which groups are vulnerable and who controls which territory. If you train two completely separate networks, you’re computing those features twice.

With a shared network, you do that expensive computation once, then have two relatively small heads: one predicts a distribution over moves, and the other predicts the value of the position. If you need both predictions, that can get you close to halving the neural-network inference cost, assuming the shared network is about the same size as either separate network.

But that doesn’t necessarily mean the whole search becomes twice as fast. It depends on how often you would have called each network and how much time you spend elsewhere in the search. There’s also a learning benefit potentially: learning which positions are good can help you learn which moves are good, and vice versa.

r001.rationale: It says a shared network computes common board features once, reducing inference cost when producing both policy and value predictions.

r002.rationale: It describes shared understanding and possible mutual learning, but does not say the policy and value predictions should give consistent evaluations of a position.

sol-6.1.text:
The policy and value networks are answering different questions, but they need a lot of the same understanding of the board. The policy asks, “What move should I consider?” and the value asks, “How good is this position?” You don’t necessarily want to compute that understanding twice.

So you can have a shared trunk with two heads. You do the expensive feature computation once, and then producing both predictions is relatively cheap. If the two separate networks were roughly the same size, you could imagine approaching a factor-of-two saving per joint evaluation, though the actual savings depend on the architecture and how often search needs each prediction.

The interesting thing is what you do with that saving. You can spend it on more search, or on a bigger network. And sharing can help learning too, because predicting good moves and predicting who wins provide related training signals. But it’s not automatic that sharing improves everything—you can also get interference between the two objectives.

r001.rationale: It says a shared trunk computes common board features once instead of computing them twice, reducing computation.

r002.rationale: It describes policy and value predictions as related, but does not state that they should provide consistent evaluations of a position.
